Volume 05 · Chapter 05

General equilibrium and welfare

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v05-c04

By the endAnalyze exchange and production interactions across markets.

One price change changes more than one market

Capability: analyze exchange and production interactions across markets. Prerequisite: competitive equilibrium and surplus, including the distinction between efficiency and distribution. We also use consumer choice and demand correspondences, duality and welfare, profit maximization, and the concavity and multiplier arguments of constrained optimization.

A higher food price raises a buyer's expenditure, but it also raises the value of a farmer's harvest. If firms use grain to produce another good, their input choices and profits change too. A general equilibrium model closes these accounts: the resources sold by one participant are acquired by another, profits belong to someone, and incomes respond to the same prices that determine demand.

All economies below are original synthetic examples. Goods are divisible, quantities refer to one specified period, and each price has units of money per unit of its commodity. A commodity includes its quality, location, delivery date and, when relevant, the state in which delivery occurs. A unit delivered only after a flood is a different commodity from an unconditional unit today. Calling two promises the same good would omit an economically relevant market.

A finite private-ownership economy

There are finitely many consumers i, commodities ℓ and firms j. Consumer i has consumption xi ∈ ℝ+L, endowment ωi ≥ 0 and preferences represented by Ui(xi). Write Ω = Σiωi for aggregate endowment. In the basic model, utility depends only on that consumer's own bundle. Any external effect will be introduced explicitly.

A firm's net-output vector yj belongs to its production set Yj. Positive coordinates are outputs; negative coordinates are inputs. Transforming 4 units of good 1 into 6 units of good 2 means y = (−4,6), not (4,6). At a common nonnegative price vector p ≠ 0, its profit is p·yj, in money. Consumer i owns share θij ≥ 0 of firm j, with Σiθij = 1 for every firm. All profits or losses must be allocated once.

Let Ti be a lump-sum transfer received by i; negative T means a payment. For a closed redistribution scheme, ΣTi = 0. The transfer is fixed independently of the consumer's chosen purchases or work. At the prices and production under consideration, the budget is

mi = p·ωi + Σjθijp·yj + Ti,
p·xi ≤ mi.

Individual mi must allow a nonempty budget. Endowment income is the value of the whole endowment, even if some of it is retained: net purchases cost p·(xi−ωi). One must not add both the endowment's value and the proceeds from selling that same endowment as separate income. A pure-exchange economy has no production terms. A private-ownership equilibrium ordinarily has Ti = 0; an equilibrium with transfers specifies them separately.

With free disposal of unused resources, feasibility is Σxi ≤ Ω + Σyj, coordinate by coordinate. A competitive or Walrasian equilibrium consists of p, all xi and all yj such that:

  1. Each firm attains a global profit maximum on Yj at p.
  2. Each consumer chooses xi ∈ Di(p,mi), taking prices, profit income and any transfer as given.
  3. Resources are feasible and every positively priced market clears: if z = Σxi−Ω−Σyj, then z ≤ 0 and pℓzℓ = 0 for every ℓ.

Zero-price goods may be left over; excess demand is never made feasible merely by assigning it price zero. With p ≫ 0, market clearing means z = 0. Price taking is a behavioral assumption even in a small teaching economy; two consumers are not automatically too small to influence actual bargaining.

With no transfers, multiplying every price by the same a > 0 multiplies endowment values and profits by a without changing budgets in real terms or firm maximizers. With transfers, their money amounts must be multiplied by a as well. We may normalize one positive price to 1 or impose Σpℓ = 1. This chooses a unit of account, not an extra economic restriction. A normalized price ratio measures units of the numeraire good per unit of another good; the model does not determine a currency's absolute purchasing-power level.

Walras law is an accounting identity, not market clearing

Suppose individual optimizing choices exist and preferences are locally nonsatiated on their consumption sets. As in c01, every chosen budget is exhausted: p·xi = mi. This follows from the small affordable improvement around any bundle with budget slack; p ≠ 0 has finite norm. Sum these equalities, use complete profit ownership and ΣTi = 0, and obtain

p·Σxi = p·Ω + Σjp·yj, hence p·z = 0.

This is Walras law. It holds even at prices where desired quantities do not clear the markets, provided the stated budgets and decisions are well defined. It balances value, not the quantity of each good. If all but market k clear, then pkzk = 0; we may infer zk = 0 only when pk > 0. For example p = (1,0), z = (0,2) satisfy the identity but not feasibility. Satiation with unspent wealth gives an inequality instead of the asserted budget-exhaustion identity; omitted profits or an unfunded transfer can also invalidate the accounting.

The actual MIT exchange-economy slides, especially slides 6 and 18–34, build relative-price determination from fixed endowments and interacting demands. Our consumer-level accounting and all calculations below are developed explicitly; we do not assume that different consumers can always be replaced by one representative consumer.

Reading an Edgeworth box

With two consumers A and B, two goods and no disposal, an allocation satisfies xB = Ω−xA. Draw a rectangle of width Ω₁ and height Ω₂. The lower-left origin belongs to A: moving right adds A's good 1 and moving up adds A's good 2. The upper-right origin belongs to B: moving left adds B's good 1 and moving down adds B's good 2. A single point specifies both bundles; it is not a graph of one consumer's quantity against the other's utility.

For Ω = (12,12), the following coordinate representation fixes both axes unambiguously. Write the plotted point as (s,t) in A's coordinates.

An Edgeworth box in coordinates; all entries are physical quantities
PointA: (s,t)B: (12−s,12−t)Interpretation
Lower-left origin(0,0)(12,12)B holds everything
Upper-right origin(12,12)(0,0)A holds everything
Endowment E(9,3)(3,9)Initial ownership
Equilibrium C(4,8)(8,4)Worked example 1
Transfer target R(2,16/3)(10,20/3)Worked example 2

At positive prices, A's budget boundary through its endowment is p₁s+p₂t = p·ωA, with slope −p₁/p₂. B's boundary becomes the same line after substituting its reversed coordinates and Ω = ωA+ωB. Their affordable sides are opposite sides of this line. At an interior equilibrium, both consumers' chosen indifference curves meet the line at the same allocation point. For smooth preferences with positive marginal utilities, both MRS values U₁/U₂ equal p₁/p₂. Corners and kinks require direct optimization or supporting inequalities; a picture of a tangency alone is not an equilibrium proof.

Worked example 1: the endowment is income at the price being solved

Let ωA = (9,3), ωB = (3,9), UA = xA1xA2² and UB = xB1²xB2. Prices are strictly positive; normalize p₂ = 1 and write p₁ = r. Income is mA = 9r+3 and mB = 3r+9. These values must move with r.

Positive incomes permit positive bundles with positive utility, while either axis gives zero utility. At a maximum both goods are therefore positive. Maximizing log utility gives A expenditure shares 1/3 and 2/3, and B shares 2/3 and 1/3. The strictly concave log objectives establish global uniqueness, including comparison with the inferior axes. Thus

xA = ((9r+3)/(3r), 2(9r+3)/3),
xB = (2(3r+9)/(3r), (3r+9)/3).

Good 1 clears if 3+1/r+2+6/r = 12, or 5+7/r = 12. Hence r = 1, mA = mB = 12, and the chosen bundles are A = (4,8), B = (8,4). Independently check good 2: 8+4 = 12. Both goods clear, both budgets are exhausted, and both bundles are individually optimal. A's net trade is (−5,+5); B's is (+5,−5). The common budget line is t = 12−s, passing through E and C in the coordinate table.

Each original utility rises from 81 to 256, a within-person ranking comparison. Equal numbers across the two utility formulas carry no interpersonal welfare meaning. In this particular economy the good-1 equation has exactly one positive solution; that proves uniqueness of its normalized positive-price equilibrium. It does not prove general equilibrium existence, uniqueness or convergence of an imagined price-adjustment process in other economies.

Pareto efficiency and the contract curve

A feasible allocation is Pareto efficient if no other feasible allocation makes every consumer at least as well off and at least one strictly better off. A Pareto improvement requires actual weak gains for all. An increase in a sum of money-valued benefits, or a hypothetical ability to compensate losers, is not by itself that improvement. Pareto efficiency is invariant to each person's strictly increasing utility transformation; a particular sum of utility numbers is not.

In a two-person exchange box, the set of efficient allocations is called the contract curve, including any efficient boundaries. It generally has many points. It is not the set of competitive equilibria for one fixed endowment, nor only the efficient points both consumers prefer to their original endowments.

At an interior efficient allocation with differentiable utility and positive marginal utilities, MRSA = MRSB is necessary. If A's MRS exceeds B's, choose a trade rate τ between them. Give a small amount ε of good 1 to A and take τε of good 2 from A. A's first-order utility change is εUA2(MRSA−τ) > 0; B's is εUB2(τ−MRSB) > 0. Interiority makes sufficiently small trades feasible, and differentiability preserves the strict signs for small ε. The opposite inequality reverses the trade. This argument establishes necessity, not unconditional sufficiency.

In Worked example 1, A's MRS at (s,t) is t/(2s); B's is 2(12−t)/(12−s). Equating them gives

t(12−s) = 4s(12−t), hence t = 16s/(4+s), 0 < s < 12.

The curve passes through C = (4,8), where both MRS values are 1. The supporting-price proof below establishes efficiency of every interior point of this curve. The endpoints (0,0) and (12,12) are also efficient: the person holding everything is strictly harmed by surrendering any positive amount of either good. Any other boundary point gives one consumer zero utility while that consumer holds a positive quantity of a useless unpaired good; transferring some of that quantity to the other consumer increases the other's utility, or both can be given positive bundles when both initially have zero utility. Such points are inefficient. The entire contract curve is therefore the displayed curve together with its two endpoints. Its extreme inequalities illustrate why efficiency alone is not a distributional recommendation.

The first welfare theorem: a value argument

Finite-economy statement. Suppose a competitive equilibrium as defined above exists. Preferences are complete, transitive and locally nonsatiated on ℝ+L; each consumer cares only about its own priced consumption; every relevant feasible trade is available at the same prices; and firms maximize profits over the correctly specified production sets. Ownership and any fixed transfers account for all wealth. Then its feasible allocation is Pareto efficient among the allocations of this economy. Convexity, differentiability and uniqueness are not additional requirements for this implication.

Here is the proof, including the step about consumers who merely remain indifferent. Let stars denote the equilibrium and set mi = p·xi*. If a bundle ai is weakly preferred to xi*, it must cost at least mi. Otherwise it has strict budget slack; local nonsatiation supplies a nearby affordable bundle strictly preferred to ai, hence to xi*, contradicting optimality. If ai is strictly preferred to the equilibrium choice, it must cost strictly more than mi, directly by consumer optimization.

Now suppose an alternative feasible allocation (a,b) Pareto dominates the equilibrium, where bj is each firm's alternative production. Summing the preceding inequalities yields Σp·ai > Σmi. Yet feasibility, nonnegative prices and firm optimality imply

Σp·ai ≤ p·Ω + Σp·bj ≤ p·Ω + Σp·yj* = Σmi.

This contradicts the strict inequality. The last equality uses complete profit ownership and balanced transfers. No convex combination or derivative entered the proof. Existence was assumed at the outset: the theorem does not produce prices or guarantee an optimizing firm when profits are unbounded. Nor does it say an efficient equilibrium is fair, compensates a policy loser, or is the allocation a social decision maker would select.

Townsend's MIT lecture on the fundamental welfare theorems, transcript pages 2–4, supplies the weak-preference cost lemma and production-value contradiction. Pages 5–12 distinguish a smooth decentralization argument from the more general supporting-price and quasiequilibrium route. The proof and scope above specify the particular finite model used here.

The second welfare theorem: support requires redistribution and conditions

The converse asks whether a selected efficient allocation can be implemented by decentralized choice after redistributing wealth. Convexity now matters. One finite-dimensional support version has consumption sets ℝ+L, continuous convex locally nonsatiated preferences, and nonempty convex production sets with free disposal. For a Pareto-efficient allocation using the aggregate resources, convex separation gives a nonzero nonnegative supporting vector p. Firms maximize p·y, and with assigned wealth mi* = p·xi*, every strictly preferred bundle ai obeys

Ui(ai) > Ui(xi*) ⇒ p·ai ≥ mi*.

This is a price quasiequilibrium with transfers. Its consumer condition is weaker than full maximization: it permits a strictly better bundle costing exactly mi*. The separating-hyperplane route puts the convex aggregate set of strictly preferred consumptions on one side of a supporting hyperplane and the convex feasible production-plus-endowment set on the other. Local nonsatiation makes the target a limiting point of the preferred set; free disposal makes support prices nonnegative. This explains the assumptions and the weak cost inequality. We do not supply the general separation theorem or graduate nonsmooth extensions here; the restricted constructive result below is proved in full.

There is a useful explicit upgrade. Suppose consumer i has a convex consumption set, continuous preferences, and some feasible-in-that-set bundle bi with p·bi < mi*. If a strictly preferred bundle ai cost exactly mi*, its mixture (1−ε)ai+εbi would remain strictly preferred for small ε > 0 by continuity but cost less than mi*, contradicting quasiequilibrium. Thus all strictly better bundles actually cost more, establishing utility maximization. With ℝ+L and positive assigned wealth, zero is a cheaper bundle. At zero wealth this argument cannot be assumed.

For example, with one consumer, ω = (0,1), U = x₁+x₂ and p = (1,0), the efficient allocation x* = (0,1) has zero wealth and satisfies the weak support condition. Every strictly better bundle costs at least zero. Nevertheless (0,2) costs zero and is better, and demand is unbounded in the free second good. These particular support prices yield a quasiequilibrium, not a competitive equilibrium. This does not say that the allocation has no other supporting equilibrium prices.

A complete constructive result for smooth interior exchange

Consider two consumers and two goods, a strictly positive resource-exhausting target, and differentiable concave utility functions with positive marginal utilities. If the target is Pareto efficient, the small-trade argument already proved equality of its MRS values. Choose p = (MRS,1). For each i, ∇Ui(xi*) = λip with λi = Ui2(xi*) > 0. Concavity's supporting inequality says that every bundle a satisfies

Ui(a) ≤ Ui(xi*) + λip·(a−xi*).

At the assigned budget mi* = p·xi*, the final term is nonpositive for every affordable a. Thus the target is a global consumer optimum. Set Ti = p·xi*−p·ωi. Resource exhaustion proves ΣTi = 0. Prices, targets and transfers now satisfy every exchange-equilibrium condition. Conversely, any resource-exhausting target satisfying these gradient and concavity conditions is supported this way and is efficient by the first theorem.

The argument also works when a concave representation is defined on strictly positive bundles and every boundary bundle ranks below the positive target, as with the log representation of our product utilities. Positive coordinates handle the differentiability step; boundary bundles must still be checked separately. More general preferences, zero consumption, zero support wealth and nonconvex production need their own conditions. A first-order match without the supporting inequality is not a proof of decentralization.

With production, the transfer accounting becomes Ti = p·xi*−p·ωi−Σθijp·yj*; one must also prove that the proposed yj* globally maximizes profit at p. Resource exhaustion again makes transfers sum to zero. Lump-sum redistribution changes purchasing power without changing marginal purchase prices. Actual tax schedules based on labor, output or spending can change incentives and require a new equilibrium analysis. The theorem neither supplies information about private preferences nor proves such transfers politically or administratively feasible.

Worked example 2: constructing the prices and transfers

Keep Worked example 1's endowments and preferences but choose the target A = (2,16/3), B = (10,20/3). It exhausts (12,12). A's MRS is (16/3)/(2·2) = 4/3; B's is 2(20/3)/10 = 4/3. Their log representations log x₁+2 log x₂ and 2 log x₁+log x₂ have negative definite diagonal Hessians on the positive orthant; every axis bundle has lower original utility than the target. The constructive argument therefore supports this efficient allocation at p = (4/3,1).

The targets cost mA* = 8 and mB* = 20. Original endowment wealth at these same prices is 15 and 13. Hence TA = −7 and TB = +7, measured in units of the good-2 numeraire. The transfers balance. A spends 8/3 on good 1 and 16/3 on good 2; B spends 40/3 on good 1 and 20/3 on good 2. These are exactly their optimizing expenditure shares. Their quantities clear both markets.

The supporting budget line in A's coordinates is t = 8−(4/3)s. Unlike the initial no-transfer budget boundary t = 15−(4/3)s, it passes through the target. Merely announcing the new price without redistributing wealth would not implement it. A's original utility falls from 256 at C to 512/9 at R, while B's rises from 256 to 2000/3. Both allocations are efficient. Moving from C to R is redistribution, not a Pareto improvement; an efficient target need not satisfy everyone's voluntary participation relative to C or to the original endowment.

Worked example 3: production, ownership and an unpriced effect

There are two goods, one firm and two consumers. Good 1 is a divisible consumption good that can also be used in production; it is the numeraire. Endowments are ωA = (12,0) and ωB = (8,0). Producing q ≥ 0 units of good 2 uses z = q²/4 units of good 1. Thus the efficient production vector is (−q²/4,q); using more input or discarding output is permitted. A owns 3/4 of profits, B owns 1/4. Utilities are UA = xA1+8 log(1+xA2) and UB = xB1+4 log(1+xB2).

Write p = (1,r), r > 0. The firm maximizes rq−q²/4. Completing the square gives r²−(q−2r)²/4, so q = 2r is the unique global optimum and profit is r². Consumers take their profit shares as given: mA = 12+3r²/4, mB = 8+r²/4.

For utility x₁+a log(1+x₂), substitute x₁ = m−rx₂. The derivative a/(1+x₂)−r is decreasing; optimal good-2 consumption is min{m/r, max{0,a/r−1}}. On a branch where both consumers retain positive good 1, good-2 demands are 8/r−1 and 4/r−1. Clearing against q = 2r gives 12/r−2 = 2r, or r²+r−6 = 0. The positive candidate is r = 2.

At that candidate q = 4, input z = 4 and profit π = 4. Wealth is (15,9), good-2 demands are (3,1), and residual good-1 demands are (9,7). Both are positive, validating the branch. Check both markets: 3+1 = 4 and 9+7+4 = 20. Total consumption expenditure is 24, equal to endowment value 20 plus profit 4. Counting the firm's revenue 8 as an extra household payment would double-count its input bill; profit is revenue 8 minus input cost 4.

If B instead owns the whole firm, at these prices wealth becomes (12,12). The unchanged good-2 demands (3,1) remain affordable, and good-1 consumption becomes (6,10). Thus the same production and prices clear, but distribution changes. Quantity neutrality here comes from quasilinearity with positive residual numeraire, not from a general claim that ownership never affects equilibrium demand.

What changes when pollution has no market?

Now let production q also create pollution q. Add −(3/5)q to A's utility and −(3/10)q to B's. Each household takes ambient pollution as given in its private purchase problem, and the firm's profit objective includes no pollution price. Ownership gives profit claims but no internalizing instruction to the firm's manager. The preceding private choices still clear the two traded markets at q = 4. They need not be efficient for the enlarged economy: utility is no longer a function of only one's own two traded goods.

To exhibit the missing gain, first allocate a fixed total q of good 2. When q ≥ 1, equal marginal benefits give 8/(1+xA2) = 4/(1+xB2) and xA2+xB2 = q. Therefore xA2 = (2q+1)/3 and xB2 = (q−1)/3. Maximizing the sum of these particular quasilinear utilities over feasible choices has derivative

12/(q+2) − q/2 − 9/10.

It is strictly decreasing and equals zero at q = 3. For 0 ≤ q ≤ 1, all good 2 goes to A and the derivative is 8/(1+q)−q/2−9/10, which remains positive through q = 1. Available input restricts q ≤ √80; the proposed q = 3 is feasible. Hence the sum's global maximum occurs at q = 3, with good-2 allocation (7/3,2/3). Strict concavity in the good-2 allocation justifies the allocation step. This sum is a convenient way to find a candidate in the specified quasilinear representations, not a general interpersonal utility metric.

At q = 3 production uses 9/4 of good 1, leaving 71/4. Assign good-1 quantities 10 to A and 31/4 to B. Compared with the private allocation (9,3) for A and (7,1) for B at pollution 4, their utility changes are

ΔUA = 8/5 − 8 log(6/5) > 0,
ΔUB = 21/20 − 4 log(6/5) > 0.

The inequalities follow from log(1+t) < t for t > 0: log(6/5) < 1/5. Both consumers actually gain and all resources balance, so this is a Pareto improvement. The first theorem has not been contradicted: its private, fully priced commodity structure omitted pollution. Designing an enforceable pollution instrument would require specifying rights, payments, information and implementation; the existence of a missing gain does not by itself provide that institution.

What these results leave open

Complete markets mean that all relevant feasible transfers have the prices and contracts used in the model. If households cannot contract on future states, efficiency relative to all state-contingent allocations may fail even while each existing spot market clears. Exercise 8 isolates that distinction. An outcome may be efficient within a restricted opportunity set while improvable in a larger technologically feasible set. Information or enforcement constraints may also restrict the planner, so the proper comparison must be stated rather than assumed.

Townsend's MIT lecture on failures of the welfare theorems, transcript pages 3–8, distinguishes nonconvex support failures, local satiation and a pollution effect absent from traded-good prices. Our solved pollution economy makes the omitted term and an actual improvement explicit; it is not an empirical environmental estimate.

Existence, uniqueness and stability are different questions. Finding one allocation that satisfies all equilibrium conditions establishes existence for that particular economy. Finding one root numerically does not rule out others; an algebraic root still needs budget, nonnegativity and global-choice checks. Welfare theorems describe qualifying equilibria, not a mechanism guaranteed to reach them. Nonconvex technologies may have efficient plans unsupported by linear prices, as Exercise 7 shows. General existence proofs, broader support theorems and dynamics are later topics, not conclusions supplied by a two-good diagram.

Exercises

  1. Audit wealth and Walras law. In Worked example 1, evaluate both incomes, both demands and aggregate excess demand at p = (2,1). Verify p·z = 0 and explain why this is not equilibrium. Normalize prices to sum to 1 and check the choices. Prove the finite production version of Walras law from household budgets and ownership shares. Explain why p = (1,0), z = (0,2) prevents an unconditional “one market is redundant” claim.
  2. Ownership can move a relative price. Keep the preferences and aggregate resources of Worked example 1, but change endowments to ωA = (6,2), ωB = (6,10). Derive the positive equilibrium with p₂ = 1, check both markets and both budgets, and interpret why aggregate physical supplies alone do not determine the same equilibrium price as before.
  3. Construct another efficient distribution. Derive the interior contract curve from both consumers' MRS expressions. Set A's good-1 quantity to 6, find the corresponding efficient allocation, and construct supporting prices with p₂ = 1 and balanced transfers from the original endowments (9,3)/(3,9). Verify individual optimization and compare each person's original product utility with the no-transfer equilibrium. Is this a Pareto improvement?
  4. Identify the indispensable step. Prove why a consumer weakly preferring a candidate bundle to its equilibrium bundle cannot buy the candidate for strictly less than equilibrium wealth under local nonsatiation. Explain why this lemma matters when only one person strictly improves. Then consider one good, endowments 1 for each of two consumers, price 1, UA = 0 at every quantity and UB(x) = x. Are choices (1,1) an equilibrium? Are they Pareto efficient? Locate the failed assumption rather than invoking convexity.
  5. Support is not yet optimal choice. For one consumer with ω = (0,1), U = x₁+x₂ and proposed prices (1,0), verify the weak support inequality at x* = (0,1), and give a preferred affordable bundle. Prove the cheaper-bundle upgrade from quasiequilibrium under continuity and a convex consumption set. Explain why it fails at these assigned prices and wealth, and exhibit other nonnegative prices that do support this same resource-efficient allocation as an equilibrium.
  6. Reconcile a new production equilibrium. In Worked example 3 remove pollution and set both log coefficients to 12. Keep endowments (12,0)/(8,0), ownership shares 3/4 and 1/4, and input cost q²/4. Solve prices, production, profit, incomes and consumption, checking the assumed positive-numeraire branch. Transfer all firm ownership to B and recheck. Explain why a zero-wealth consumer would invalidate the uncapped log-demand formula.
  7. An efficient production plan with no price support. One consumer owns a firm and has endowment (4,0) and utility U = x₁+√x₂. The firm can use z ∈ [0,2] of good 1 to produce q ≤ z² of good 2; inputs or outputs may be freely discarded. Show that the plan z = 1, q = 1 and consumption (3,1) is Pareto efficient for this one-consumer economy. Show the production set is nonconvex. Prove that no nonzero nonnegative linear prices can make that firm plan profit maximizing, even with a household wealth transfer. Do not infer that the first welfare theorem requires convexity.
  8. A missing insurance market. There are two equally probable future states and one consumption good in each. A's endowment across states is (9,1), B's is (1,9). Both have expected utility (log c₁+log c₂)/2. There is no storage or production. With no advance contingent contracts, each can only consume its own realized endowment in a one-good spot market. Calculate expected utilities. Show that (5,5) for each person is feasible and strictly preferred before the state is known. If enforceable claims for both states can be traded in advance, verify equilibrium at state prices (1,1), including wealth and demands. State the information/enforcement assumptions behind the improvement and distinguish ex ante welfare from an ex post comparison in one realized state.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria
  1. At (2,1), mA = 21 and mB = 15. A demands (7/2,14) and B demands (5,5); their costs are 7+14 = 21 and 10+5 = 15. Aggregate demand is (17/2,19), so z = (−7/2,7) and p·z = −7+7 = 0. There is excess supply of good 1 and excess demand of good 2, so neither value balance nor budget exhaustion establishes feasibility. Dividing prices by 3 gives (2/3,1/3), wealth (7,5), and identical real budgets and choices. In production, sum p·xi = p·ωi+Σjθijp·yj+Ti. Since each firm's ownership sums to 1 and total transfers are zero, Σp·xi = p·Ω+Σp·yj; subtract to obtain p·z = 0. This uses individual exhaustion, not an assumption of aggregate clearing. At p = (1,0) the second excess demand has zero value and is invisible to the identity. An omitted market clears by division only when its price is strictly positive.
  2. At p = (r,1), wealth is (6r+2,6r+10). Good-1 demand is (6r+2)/(3r)+2(6r+10)/(3r) = 6+22/(3r). Equating it to 12 gives r = 11/9. Wealth is (28/3,52/3). Demands are A = (28/11,56/9) and B = (104/11,52/9). Good 1 sums to 132/11 = 12 and good 2 to 108/9 = 12. A spends 28/9+56/9 = 28/3; B spends 104/9+52/9 = 52/3. All quantities are positive and the strictly concave log problems justify the same share rules. Different consumers have different expenditure shares. Moving endowments changes their wealth at each candidate price and therefore aggregate demand, even with fixed total quantities. The new relative price 11/9 differs from 1; no representative-consumer invariance was assumed.
  3. At A = (s,t), B = (12−s,12−t), so MRS equality is t/(2s) = 2(12−t)/(12−s). Rearranging yields t = 16s/(4+s). At s = 6, A = (6,48/5), B = (6,12/5). The common MRS is 4/5, giving p = (4/5,1). Target wealth is (72/5,36/5), while original endowment wealth is (51/5,57/5). Thus T = (+21/5,−21/5), summing to zero. A spends (24/5,48/5) in its 1:2 ratio; B spends (24/5,12/5) in its 2:1 ratio. The original utilities of positive bundles are maximized by the strictly concave log objectives at these budgets; axes yield zero. Feasibility and the first theorem establish efficiency. A's product utility is 6(48/5)² = 13824/25 > 256, while B's is 6²(12/5) = 432/5 < 256. B loses, so this is not a Pareto improvement. Comparing each number with that same person's baseline is valid; comparing the two persons' utility levels directly is unnecessary.
  4. Let a be weakly preferred to equilibrium x* and suppose p·a < m. Choose ε < (m−p·a)/‖p‖. Every nonnegative point within ε of a is affordable. Local nonsatiation supplies one strictly preferred to a, which by transitivity is strictly preferred to x*, contradicting its optimality. Thus p·a ≥ m. Without this result, spending reductions by merely indifferent people might offset the higher cost of the strictly improved person's bundle, destroying the aggregate contradiction. In the one-good case each consumer's budget is x ≤ 1. A can optimally choose 1 because every choice ties; B optimally chooses 1. Choices clear, so (1,1) is an equilibrium. Allocation (0,2) is feasible, leaves A indifferent and strictly improves B, so the equilibrium is inefficient. A is locally satiated everywhere. Preferences and feasible sets are convex; convexity does not repair this missing first-theorem hypothesis.
  5. The proposed wealth is p·ω = 0. Every nonnegative bundle, including every strictly preferred one, has cost x₁ ≥ 0, so the weak support condition holds. Yet (0,2) costs zero and raises utility from 1 to 2; there is no maximizing bundle because free x₂ can grow without bound. For the upgrade, suppose a strictly preferred bundle a costs exactly m and b in the consumption set costs less than m. Convexity keeps (1−ε)a+εb in the set; continuity keeps it strictly preferred for sufficiently small positive ε. Its cost is strictly below m, contradicting the quasiequilibrium inequality. Strictly preferred bundles costing less were already excluded, so all strictly preferred bundles cost more and the target is optimal. At (1,0) and m = 0 there is no cheaper nonnegative bundle, so this proof cannot be applied. Prices (1,1) give wealth 1; every bundle with x₁+x₂ = 1 maximizes U, including (0,1), which clears the resource markets at the chosen allocation. Thus the example concerns defective support prices, not an impossibility of all equilibrium support.
  6. Supply is q = 2r and profit r². On the proposed interior branch, each consumer demands 12/r−1 of good 2. Clearing gives 24/r−2 = 2r, or r²+r−12 = 0. The positive solution is r = 3; q = 6, input is 9 and profit is 18−9 = 9. Wealth is mA = 12+27/4 = 75/4 and mB = 8+9/4 = 41/4. Both buy 3 units of good 2, costing 9 each. Residual good-1 consumption is (39/4,5/4), both positive. Good-1 consumption plus input is 44/4+9 = 20, and good 2 clears at 6. Total expenditure is 29 = 20+9. If B owns all profits, wealth becomes (12,17), and consumption becomes A = (3,3), B = (8,3). Both numeraire holdings remain positive and the same prices and output clear. If a consumer has zero endowment wealth and no profits or transfers, its positive-price budget allows only zero; 12/r−1 could be positive but unaffordable. The correct demand is capped by m/r, and the candidate aggregate equation must be changed when that cap binds.
  7. For any feasible production and allocation, x₁ ≤ 4−z and x₂ ≤ z² for some z ∈ [0,2]. Hence U ≤ 4−z+√(z²) = 4, attained at (3,1), so this one-person allocation is Pareto efficient. The feasible production vectors (0,0) and (−2,4) have midpoint (−1,2), which is infeasible: with input at most 1 output cannot exceed 1. Free disposal does not create it. At prices (a,b) ≥ 0, profit from the target plan is b−a. To beat the zero plan requires b ≥ a; to beat the plan (−2,4) requires b−a ≥ 4b−2a, or a ≥ 3b. Together a ≤ b ≤ a/3 force a = b = 0, excluded. Thus no nonzero nonnegative prices support the target firm's choice. A lump-sum household transfer cannot change these firm profit comparisons. Nonconvexity defeats this converse support claim; the first theorem would still establish efficiency of any equilibrium satisfying its other hypotheses.
  8. At their endowments each has expected utility (log 9+log 1)/2 = log 3. Consumption (5,5) for each uses all 10 units in each state and gives log 5, a strict gain log(5/3). At state prices (1,1), each endowment has date-of-contract value 10. The strictly concave log objective gives equal expenditure on the two positive state claims, so each demands (5,5); both state markets clear. The net claims of A are (−4,+4), and B's are opposite; each is worth zero at these prices. The construction assumes common known state probabilities, advance commitment, verifiable states and deliveries, enforceable transfers, no default or transaction cost, and that these transfers are feasible. In the high-endowment state an individual gives up 4 units, so the realized comparison need not improve that individual's consumption. The Pareto gain is ex ante according to the specified expected utilities. Existing spot-market clearing alone cannot establish efficiency relative to contracts excluded from that market structure; if the planner also cannot enforce them, that restriction changes the relevant feasible comparison.

Teach-back and Delayed check

Teach-back: explain why selling an endowment and receiving firm profits must be accounted for without duplication. Use the two origins of the Edgeworth box to explain a common budget line, then prove the first theorem without drawing an indifference curve. Explain why the second theorem adds convexity, transfers and support qualifications, and why an efficient distribution need not be a Pareto improvement on another efficient distribution.

Delayed check: two consumers both have U = x₁x₂, with endowments (6,0) and (0,4). Normalize p₂ = 1. Solve the positive-price exchange equilibrium, check both budgets and markets, and state why Walras law alone would not verify a zero-price omitted market.

Delayed-check answer

At p₁ = r, wealth is (6r,4). Equal expenditure gives A = (3,3r), B = (2/r,2). Good 1 clears when 3+2/r = 6, so r = 2/3. Wealth is 4 for each, both consume (3,2), and good 2 clears at 4. Each bundle costs 2+2 = 4. A positive omitted price permits division of pkzk = 0; a zero price does not. Prices, endowment wealth, optimization and physical resources must all agree.

The next chapter, monopoly, oligopoly and pricing, changes the assumption that firms take output prices as given. Keep separate the existence of an equilibrium, its efficiency within a specified feasible set, and the distribution it implements: none is a substitute for the others.

Sources and further study

  • Arnaud Costinot, MIT 14.54: Lecture 4, Exchange Economies (Fall 2016) — Method route for fixed-endowment economies, relative prices, trade and simultaneous market consistency; endowment-sensitive aggregate demand when preferences differ.
  • Robert M. Townsend, MIT 14.04: Lecture 16, Fundamental Welfare Theorems (Fall 2020), official transcript — Primary lecture content on the finite first-theorem value proof, smooth supporting-price and wealth-transfer construction, and the weaker consumer condition in price quasiequilibrium.
  • Robert M. Townsend, MIT 14.04: Lecture 20, Failure of Welfare Theorems (Fall 2020), official transcript — Method scope for nonconvex support failures, local satiation and pollution omitted from private commodity prices; distinction between price-taking private choices and the larger feasible welfare comparison.
